whenValue.say: That is the sensitivity, $\P(\text{positive} \mid \text{has it})$ — which was given to you. The question asks for the reverse conditional, and those two are different numbers whenever the condition is rare.

That is the sensitivity you were given, $\P(\text{positive} \mid \text{has it})$. You are being asked for $\P(\text{has it} \mid \text{positive})$ — the bar has been turned round, and Bayes is what turns it.
That is the specificity, which is about people who do *not* have the condition. It is one of the inputs, not the answer.
That is the prevalence — the probability *before* the test. The test must move it somewhat; the question is how far.
Close to the right shape. Check the denominator: it has to be the total number of positives, from both the people who have it and the people who do not.

feedback.nudge: The four given numbers are all conditionals pointing the *other* way, or a base rate. Try a population of $20\,000$ people and count the positives in two groups — the ones who have it and the ones who do not.

explanation:
## By counting

Take $20{,}000$ people:

| | positive | negative | total |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **has it** | $99$ | $1$ | $100$ |
| **does not** | $995$ | $18{,}905$ | $19{,}900$ |
| **total** | $1{,}094$ | $18{,}906$ | $20{,}000$ |

$$\P(\text{has it} \mid +) = \frac{99}{1094} \approx 0.0905.$$

**About nine percent.** A positive result on a very good test still leaves it more likely than not that you do not have the condition.

## By the theorem

$$\P(D \mid +) = \frac{\P(+ \mid D)\,\P(D)}{\P(+ \mid D)\P(D) + \P(+ \mid D^c)\P(D^c)} = \frac{0.99 \times 0.005}{0.99 \times 0.005 + 0.05 \times 0.995} = \frac{99}{1094}.$$

## Why it is so much lower than $99\%$

Because there are two hundred times as many healthy people as affected ones, and $5\%$ of a very large group outnumbers $99\%$ of a very small one. $995$ false positives against $99$ true ones.

This is the **base-rate fallacy**, and the reversal it depends on has a name: $\P(+ \mid D)$ and $\P(D \mid +)$ are not the same number and are not close. Confusing them is called the *prosecutor's fallacy* when it happens in court — "the chance of this match if he were innocent is one in a million" is not "the chance he is innocent is one in a million".

## The useful way to hold it

Odds form. Prior odds $1 : 199$. Likelihood ratio $0.99 : 0.05$, which is about $19.8$. Posterior odds $19.8 : 199$, or about $1 : 10$ — roughly a $9\%$ chance. A test moves your odds by a factor; it does not hand you a probability.

## And the follow-up worth doing

Screen only people with symptoms, so the prevalence is $1$ in $10$ rather than $1$ in $200$, and the same test gives $\P(D \mid +) \approx 0.69$. The test did not change. Who you point it at did.
